extracted.intended_audience: researchers and dataset creators working on meme classification, multimodal NLP, and computational memetics
extracted.subtask_description: Define what counts as an internet meme (particularly multimodal image+text samples) and provide a repeatable protocol and typology to identify memetic content when constructing meme datasets for affective/multimodal classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifman’s definition of Internet memes
rubrics_metrics.description: An internet meme is a group of digital items that: (a) share common characteristics of content, form, and/or stance; (b) are created with awareness of each other; and (c) are circulated, imitated, and transformed via the Internet by multiple users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the foundational conceptual definition: memetics (imitation+transformation) is central. Distinguish memes from virals: virals may be popular but do not inspire derivatives. The three components (content/form/stance) guide what to look for when identifying shared characteristics across items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic Element (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A memetic element is a textual or visual element that is observably reused in multiple distinct memes (e.g., a reused background template, a recurring foreground character, a transferred visual symbol, or repeated text phrasing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A memetic element is the concrete signal used to establish that content is memetic: it must be demonstrably reused across distinct items. Examples: Socially Awkward Penguin background, Disaster Girl face, recurring text phrases. The presence of at least one memetic element in a candidate item is necessary to identify it as a meme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related-but-distinct requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Related but distinct memes are pairs/groups that share common memetic elements but differ by some novel element(s) (e.g., different captions, altered foregrounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To verify an element is memetic, find at least one other item that shares that element yet is distinct in some novel way. This establishes derivation/imitation rather than mere duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal criterion for multimodal Internet memes (proposed definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multimodal user-generated piece of digital content that contains at least one visual or textual component that can be identified as a memetic element that is shared with other related but distinct memes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational definition is intended for dataset construction: treat an image file as a candidate meme and verify memetic elements via search for related-but-distinct items. If none are found, classify as non-memetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality is not sufficient/necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Modality (visual, textual, or multimodal) alone does not determine memetic status: memes can be unimodal (text-only or image-only) or multimodal, and not all multimodal content is memetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat 'image + text overlay' as a proxy for memetic status. Identification must rely on memetic elements and evidence of reuse, not merely modality.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-derivative sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of content requires only a single derivative/instance of reuse to qualify as a meme (i.e., one related-but-distinct item sharing an element is sufficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require global popularity; emerging or culturally specific memes with limited spread can be bona fide memes if at least one derivative exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology — Template Memes (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template Memes are memes that use identical visual backgrounds as templates which are reused across related-but-distinct memes, often with different textual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly found on meme-generator sites. If reverse-image search returns visually similar images that share the same background but differ in captions/foregrounds, classify as a Template Meme. Template Memes have two common subtypes: Character Macro and Format Macro.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology — Character Macro (CM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character Macro memes are template memes centred around a distinctive character (image) with superimposed text captions that signify stereotypical behaviour or a recurring trope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify by cropping to remove textual overlays and running reverse-image search on the character/background; finding other memes that use the same character/background but different captions indicates CM membership (e.g., Socially Awkward Penguin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology — Format Macro (FM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Format Macro memes use a visual template where meaning is conveyed through relative positions of visual and textual elements; the visual layout plus positional text create a reusable metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify by inspecting the overall visual format (e.g., multi-panel layouts, positional metaphors) and searching for other items that reuse the same positional/format structure with altered text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology — Memetic Images (MI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic Image memes are images appended with a whitespace containing a text caption; the same image is reused with multiple different captions such that the image functions as a memetic element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crop out the whitespace/caption and reverse-image search the remaining image; if multiple distinct captions are applied to that same image across results, classify as a Memetic Image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology — Transferred Symbols (TS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferred Symbols memes rely on conventionalised visual elements (symbols, characters, image segments) that have acquired meaning within meme culture and are pasted/transferred onto new backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crop the suspected symbol/segment and reverse-image search it; if it appears across varied backgrounds or paired with different segments/text, it functions as a transferred memetic symbol. This covers foreground elements reused independently of templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology — Memetic Trend (MT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic Trend memes share similar textual content or a trend-driven pattern across visually dissimilar items; the memetic element is the repeated phrasing/response rather than a consistent visual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract textual elements and perform text-based search; if the same or largely identical text appears across many visually different items (a participative trend), classify as a Memetic Trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme Identification Protocol (stepwise)
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeatable 8-step protocol using reverse-image-search (IS) and text-search (TS) to identify whether a candidate image (C) is a meme and to assign it a typology (Template/CM/FM/MI/TS/MT) or mark it non-memetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Protocol summary (apply in order):
1) Run IS(C) to find visually similar images; if any share the same background but differ in foreground/caption → Template Meme. Else:
2) Inspect overall format: character-centred → step 3; multi-segment → step 4; image+whitespace → step 5; otherwise → step 6.
3) Crop to remove text (c_crop) and IS(c_crop); matching backgrounds with different foregrounds → Character Macro.
4) Crop into visual segments (c_m) and IS(c_m); if segments pair with other segments/texts → Transferred Symbols.
5) Crop out whitespace to get c_img and IS(c_img); if same image used with different captions → Memetic Image.
6) Crop superimposed visual elements (c_elem) and IS(c_elem); if reused elsewhere → Transferred Symbols.
7) Extract text (c_text) and run TS(c_text); if identical/near-identical text appears across many visually dissimilar images → Memetic Trend.
8) If none of the above yield related-but-distinct items, classify as non-memetic.
Use this exact order and cropping/search heuristics to remove reliance on annotator familiarity. Document search results/URLs as evidence that a memetic element was found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational rule: classify as meme only if related-but-distinct item found
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate is to be considered a meme only if search evidence reveals at least one related-but-distinct meme that shares a memetic element; absence of such evidence implies non-memetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule removes subjective judgement: do not rely on annotator intuition alone. Record the supporting search result(s). If searches only return duplicates of the candidate (same image identical across sources), treat it as viral/non-memetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual search engines rather than static reference sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer reverse-image and text search engines (e.g., Google Image Search) to detect memetic reuse across the wider web rather than relying on a finite reference collection of known meme templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: memetic elements constantly evolve and many are culturally specific or emerging; static reference lists will miss non-English or new memes. Use cropping and targeted searches to find reused sub-elements. Keep records of search queries and results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation constraint for current datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: The protocol and typology are designed specifically for multimodal meme datasets where each sample is an image file containing visual and textual content (text embedded in the image).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If textual content appears outside the image (e.g., post body), the protocol may miss memetic relationships; adapt searches to include surrounding post text or platform metadata if available. When building datasets limited to image files, accept this limitation and document it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetics vs Virality distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A meme is distinguished from a viral in that a meme inspires imitations/remixes (derivatives), whereas a viral is a widely circulated singular unit that does not produce derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When search results are identical duplicates of the same image with no variants, lean towards classifying as viral/non-memetic. Look for evidence of imitation, remixing, or template-based reuse to support memetic classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyed dataset filtration criteria (reported by prior works) — NOT memetics-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical filtration criteria observed in prior meme datasets include: multimodality requirement (image+text in same image file); language filters (English-only, Bengali-only, Italian-only, code-mixed); readable text; contains text; clear background picture; contains both text and visual content; excludes cartoons/diagrams/graphs/tables; minimum image resolution; maximum text length; text in particular scripts; collected from public domains; original image must be replaceable while preserving meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria were commonly used by dataset authors but the paper critiques them as not directly relating to memetics (i.e., they do not verify that content was created via imitation/variation). When constructing meme datasets for memetics-aware tasks, do not rely solely on these filters; instead apply the memetic-element-based protocol. If you use these filters, document them explicitly and note they do not guarantee memetic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator-independence and documentation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Meme identification should not rely purely on annotator familiarity or subjective judgement; the protocol requires verifiable search evidence and documentation of related-but-distinct items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dataset repeatability, record the IS/TS queries, top matching results, crops used, timestamps, and URLs that demonstrate reuse. Provide annotator instructions to follow the protocol steps and record outcomes rather than relying on intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and edge-cases to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical challenges include culturally-specific or non-English memes, newly emerging memes with few derivatives, translation pairs (same memetic image with different-language captions), and multimodal content where text appears outside the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address these by using broad visual/text search strategies, allowing a single derivative to suffice, and explicitly documenting language/script issues. Note that static reference sets will likely miss such cases; visual search is recommended. For translated pairs, decide and document whether language variants count as distinct memes or the same meme in different languages.
